newsitem.title: USA: Hill & Knowlton dismissed from part of smoking case.
newsitem.headline: Hill & Knowlton dismissed from part of smoking case.

text.p: The Hill and Knowlton company, which for decades helped promote smoking, was partially dismissed Monday from Florida's billion-dollar Medicaid lawsuit against tobacco companies.

Palm Beach County Circuit Judge Harold Cohen ruled that the public relations firm could not be held liable for health injuries suffered by thousands of Medicaid patients because it was never involved in the manufacture or sale of cigarettes.

However, Cohen left open the possibilty that Hill and Knowlton could be held liable for triple damages for its advertising efforts on behalf of the tobacco companies -- if Florida is successful in proving cigarette makers engaged in a criminal racketeering effort.

In one of a series of pretrial hearings, the judge left it for the jury to decide whether Hill and Knowlton should be forced to give back all of the money it made from its advertising efforts from the early 1950s to 1963 as well as in 1977 and 1988.

Florida wants this money to help pay for an anti-smoking campaign aimed at young people. The case is scheduled to go to trial Aug. 4 and will be one of the first state Medicaid cases to be tried. Cohen said he was leaning toward dismissing racketeering

charges against Hill and Knowlton. However, he agreed to hold off on his ruling until Florida has a chance to present evidence relating to racketeering Tuesday at the request of one of Florida's attorneys, W. C. Gentry.
"I would like to see Hill and Knowlton remain in the lawsuit because they are bad guys. We don't believe they should be let off," Gentry said.
"The evidence will show the tobacco companies and Hill and Knowlton engaged in a Cosa Nostra-type of conspiracy."
A Hill and Knowlton attorney, Stanley Beiley, said: "I am extremely hopeful that he (Cohen) will dismiss the racketeering charges. There's no substance to them."
